hook.text: One husband, four wives. Or one wife, two husbands. Monogamy is common today, but historically it was the minority.

buildup.text: Polygamy means multiple spouses. Polygyny is one man with multiple wives; polyandry is one woman with multiple husbands.

discovery.text: Polygyny is far more common and often linked to wealth, status, and labor needs. Polyandry is rare but well-documented.

twist.text: In Tibetan polyandry, brothers share a wife to keep family land intact. It's an economic strategy, not a romantic one.

climax.text: Marriage forms reflect economic and social conditions. Monogamy, polygyny, and polyandry each solve different problems.

punchline.text: Marriage adapts to what a society needs.

details.summary: Polygamy allows marriage to multiple spouses simultaneously. Polygyny, where one man has multiple wives, is far more common cross-culturally than polyandry, where one woman has multiple husbands. Both forms reflect economic and social conditions.
details.whyItMatters: Most human societies historically permitted polygamy, making Western-style monogamy the statistical exception. Understanding polygamy reveals how marriage adapts to economic pressures, labor needs, and demographic realities.
takeaways: Polygyny is permitted in most historically documented societies
Polyandry is rare and often linked to scarce resources
Economic and ecological factors strongly influence marriage forms

faq.question: Why is polygyny more common than polyandry?
faq.answer: Polygyny often correlates with agricultural economies where more wives mean more labor and more children. Polyandry typically appears in harsh environments where resources are scarce and multiple husbands share the cost of supporting one household, as among Tibetan groups.

faq.question: Does permission for polygamy mean most people practice it?
faq.answer: No. Even in societies that permit polygyny, most men have one wife because acquiring multiple wives requires significant wealth. Polygyny is often a marker of elite status rather than a common practice for the majority.
